name: Slope
description: How steep a line is; measures rate of change

content.overview: You know that feeling when a hiking trail suddenly gets brutal? That's slope. On a graph, slope is just a number that tells you how steep the line is — and in physics, that steepness usually means something real, like how fast you're moving. {{viz:diagram-01}}
content.explanation:
Here's the deal: slope tells you how much Y changes every time X changes by 1 unit.

**The formula:** slope = (Y₂ − Y₁) / (X₂ − X₁), or the way everyone actually remembers it — rise over run.

Picture climbing a hill. Rise is how much higher you got, run is how far forward you walked. Divide one by the other and boom, that's your slope — a single number describing how brutal (or gentle) the climb is.

**Why physics is obsessed with slope:** {{viz:chart-01}}
- On a distance-time graph, slope = speed (how fast you're covering ground)
- On a velocity-time graph, slope = acceleration (how fast your speed itself is changing)
- Steep slope = things are changing fast
- Flat slope = barely any change at all
- Negative slope = you're going backwards, or the value is dropping

**Quick gut-check examples:**
- Slope of 5? For every 1 step right, you climb 5 up. Steep!
- Slope of 0? Totally flat — nothing's changing.
- Slope of −2? For every 1 step right, you drop 2. You're losing ground. {{viz:anim-01}}

At the end of the day, slope is just a number that answers "how fast is this changing?" Simple idea, but it shows up absolutely everywhere in physics.
keyPoints: Slope = rise / run = how much Y changes for every step in X
Steep slope means things are changing quickly
Flat slope means things are barely changing
Negative slope means the value is decreasing
In physics, slope often IS speed or acceleration — it's not just abstract math
On a straight line, the slope is the same no matter where you measure it
content.whyItMatters: Slope is basically how physics measures "how fast." Speed, acceleration, all the rate-of-change stuff you'll meet later — it all comes back to reading a slope off a graph. Nail this now and a lot of future topics get way less scary.
